standard_text: Make tables of equivalent ratios relating quantities with whole-number measurements, find missing values in the tables, and plot the pairs of values on the coordinate plane.

progression.narrative: 6.RP.3 asks students to do three connected things with equivalent ratios: MAKE tables of them, FIND missing values inside those tables, and PLOT the pairs on the coordinate plane. The logic runs from language to structure to picture. First a student has to know what a ratio names -- and in particular whether it compares a part to another part or a part to the whole (S1), because a table is meaningless if the two columns' meanings are fuzzy. Then comes the single engine that powers the whole standard: two ratios are equivalent exactly when BOTH parts are multiplied by the same number (S2). A ratio table is just that idea written in rows, so finding a missing value (S3) means finding the multiplier for a row -- the place where the additive shortcut ('the columns go up by the same amount') breaks students. Recognizing whether a whole table keeps one constant ratio (S4) generalizes the row-level move to the table level. Once the table is solid, the standard turns it into a picture: each row (x, y) becomes a point, and equivalent ratios plot as a straight line of points heading through the origin (S5). With table and graph both available, students use them to solve real problems -- scaling a recipe or a price up to a target value (S6). Finally, the standard looks forward: comparing two different ratio tables and catching errors in someone else's table or plot (S7), the bridge toward grade 7's unit-rate work.

steps.rationale: Name what a ratio compares. Before tables make sense, a student must tell a part-to-part ratio (3 red : 5 blue) from a part-to-whole ratio (3 red : 8 marbles) -- the columns of every later table carry these meanings.
The engine of the standard: two ratios are equivalent exactly when both parts are multiplied by the same number. Every row of every ratio table is one application of this move.
The standard's literal demand: find missing values in a ratio table. The move is 'find the row's multiplier, then multiply the other column' -- the first place the additive shortcut visibly fails.

Zoom out from one row to the whole table: a true ratio table keeps ONE constant ratio in every row. Students judge whether two tables show the same relationship and construct tables from a given ratio.
The standard's third demand: each table row (x, y) becomes a point, and equivalent ratios plot as points on a straight line through the origin. The graph is the table made visible.
Put the tools to work: extend a table (or read its graph) to reach a target value in a real context -- recipes, prices, distances. This is the standard's 'relating quantities' payoff.
Looking forward: compare two different ratio tables and analyze errors in tables and plots. Judging WHICH relationship is stronger previews grade 7 unit rates.

skills.name: Write a ratio from a described group of objects

prerequisite_skill.description: Count two groups of objects and compare them with words (more, fewer, for every)
prerequisite_skill.check_question: There are 3 cats and 5 dogs. Say a sentence comparing the cats to the dogs.

skills.i_do_script: Before any numbers move, the question's own phrase builds two labeled slots in order -- first word named, first slot. Each amount can only sit in the slot wearing its name, no matter what order the story listed things. Today we're turning a plain sentence into a ratio. If a fish tank has 3 goldfish and 4 guppies, the ratio of goldfish to guppies is 3:4 -- the first word named goes first, the second word named goes second. I always underline the two things being compared and write them in the exact order they were asked for.

canonical_error.pattern: Writes the two numbers in the order they appear in the story instead of the order the question asks for
canonical_error.example: Story says '5 dogs and 2 cats'; question asks for cats to dogs; student writes 5:2 instead of 2:5
canonical_error.why: The student copies numbers left-to-right off the page instead of matching each number to its label. They haven't internalized that a ratio's order carries meaning.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- check the order the question asks for.
redirect_script.prompt: Underline the two words in the QUESTION, in order. Now find the number that belongs to the first word and write it first.
redirect_script.praise: You matched each number to its word -- that's exactly what ratio order means.

skills.item_template: A one-sentence scenario naming two whole-number quantities (both under 25). Student writes the ratio in a:b form in the order the question asks. Numeric response, no choices; stems short enough for fluency sprints.

sample_items.stem: 3 cats and 5 dogs. Ratio of cats to dogs?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 5:3 if the student flips the order

sample_items.stem: 7 boys and 4 girls. Ratio of boys to girls?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 4:7 if the student flips the order

sample_items.stem: 2 red marbles and 9 blue. Red to blue?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 9:2 from copying the bigger number first

sample_items.stem: 6 pencils and 5 pens. Pencils to pens?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 5:6 from flipping the order

sample_items.stem: 4 wins and 3 losses. Wins to losses?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 3:4 from flipping; 4:7 if student compares wins to all games

sample_items.stem: 8 roses and 3 daisies. Roses to daisies?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 3:8 from flipping the order

sample_items.stem: 5 cups flour and 2 cups sugar. Flour to sugar?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 2:5 from flipping the order

sample_items.stem: 1 teacher and 24 students. Teacher to students?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 24:1 from writing the bigger number first

sample_items.stem: 9 apples and 7 bananas. Bananas to apples?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 9:7 from copying story order instead of question order

sample_items.stem: 6 dogs and 10 cats. Cats to dogs?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 6:10 from copying story order instead of question order

sample_items.stem: 3 green and 4 yellow apples. Green to yellow?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 4:3 from flipping the order

sample_items.stem: 12 markers and 5 crayons. Markers to crayons?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 5:12 from flipping the order

sample_items.stem: 2 goldfish and 7 snails. Snails to goldfish?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 2:7 from copying story order instead of question order

sample_items.stem: 8 vans and 15 cars. Vans to cars?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 15:8 from writing the bigger number first

vocabulary.definition: A comparison of two quantities, written like 3:5, 3 to 5, or 3/5.
An amount of something you can count or measure.
In a ratio, which number comes first -- it must match which thing was named first.

next_steps.if_fail: Practice matching each number to its label with real objects (counters in two colors) before writing any ratios.

worked_example_script.text: Before touching the story's numbers, write the question's phrase 'comic books to chapter books' and draw an empty slot under each word. The phrase built two labeled parking spots in a fixed order -- the 4 can only park under 'comic books' and the 7 can only park under 'chapter books.'
Write on the board: 'A shelf has 4 comic books and 7 chapter books.' Below it write the question: 'What is the ratio of comic books to chapter books?'
Which two things is the question comparing? Say them in the order the QUESTION uses.
Underline 'comic books' first and 'chapter books' second in the question.
How many comic books? That number goes first. How many chapter books? That goes second. So what's the ratio?
Watch for 7:4 -- that means the student copied the bigger number or the story order. Ask: 'Which word did the question say first?'
Order is the whole point of a ratio. 4:7 says 4 comics for every 7 chapter books. 7:4 would describe a totally different shelf.
Now flip it: what is the ratio of chapter books to comic books? What changed and why?
Try one alone: 5 forks and 8 spoons -- ratio of spoons to forks?

skills.name: Plot and name points in the first quadrant

prerequisite_skill.description: Graph points in the first quadrant of the coordinate plane and name plotted points (5.CA.11)
prerequisite_skill.check_question: To plot the point (2, 5), which way do you move first, and how far?

skills.i_do_script: Two moves done in the wrong order land you on a different dot: 'right 2 then up 5' and 'right 5 then up 2' are two different addresses on the grid. That's why the pair comes with a fixed order built in. We're plotting points like (3, 4). The first number is the x-coordinate -- how far I walk RIGHT from the origin along the floor. The second is the y-coordinate -- how far I climb UP. I say 'run before you jump': right 3, up 4, dot. The order never changes.

canonical_error.pattern: Reverses the coordinates -- moves up by the first number and right by the second
canonical_error.example: Asked to plot (2, 6), the student goes up 2 and right 6, landing on (6, 2)
canonical_error.why: The student knows a point needs two moves but hasn't anchored the convention that the FIRST number is always horizontal. Both moves feel interchangeable to them.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on -- which number moves you sideways?
redirect_script.prompt: Remember the two dots: (2, 5) and (5, 2) sit in different places, so the order of your moves decides where you land. Put your pencil on the origin. Say 'run, then jump': slide RIGHT the first number, then UP the second number. Trace it with your finger before you draw the dot.
redirect_script.praise: Right first, up second -- you followed the ordered pair exactly.

skills.item_template: A first-quadrant coordinate grid (ranges 0-8 or smaller). Student either names a plotted point as an ordered pair or describes/executes the moves to plot a given pair. MC or short response.

sample_items.stem: Which ordered pair names point P?
sample_items.distractor_logic: (4, 3) reverses the coordinates; the others misread one axis

sample_items.stem: Which ordered pair names point A?
sample_items.distractor_logic: (2, 5) reverses the coordinates

sample_items.stem: To plot (2, 6), how far do you move right, and how far up?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Right 6, up 2 if the student reverses the coordinates

sample_items.stem: Point B is at (4, 0). Is B on the x-axis or the y-axis?
sample_items.distractor_logic: y-axis if the student thinks the 0 controls the horizontal move

sample_items.stem: Which ordered pair names point Q?
sample_items.distractor_logic: (5, 1) reverses the coordinates

sample_items.stem: When you plot (6, 3), which number tells you how far RIGHT to go?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 3 if the student reverses the roles of the coordinates

sample_items.stem: Which ordered pair names point R?
sample_items.distractor_logic: (3, 0) reverses the coordinates; a point on the y-axis has x = 0

sample_items.stem: Which ordered pair names point M?
sample_items.distractor_logic: (1, 7) reverses the coordinates; (6, 1) misreads the x-axis by one

vocabulary.definition: Two numbers (x, y) that locate a point: right x, up y.
The corner point (0, 0) where the two axes meet -- every plot starts there.
The horizontal number line; the first coordinate moves along it.
The vertical number line; the second coordinate moves along it.

next_steps.if_fail: Practice 'run, then jump' on a floor grid or large grid paper with single points until the order is automatic.

worked_example_script.text: Show two dots on the same grid: one from 'right 2, up 5' and one from 'right 5, up 2.' Same two numbers, different places -- so the order of the two moves must matter.
Draw a first-quadrant grid from 0 to 6 on both axes. Write the ordered pair (2, 5) beside it.
A point needs two moves. Which number do you think moves us sideways, and which moves us up?
The rule never changes: the FIRST number runs right along the x-axis, the SECOND jumps up. I say 'run before you jump.'
Start a finger at the origin (0, 0). Slide right 2, then up 5. Mark the dot and label it (2, 5).
Where would (5, 2) land? Is it the same point?
If a student says (5, 2) and (2, 5) are the same point, have them plot both and compare -- the difference IS the lesson.
What about (0, 4) -- how far right do we run? So where does it sit?
Plot (4, 1) on your own, and narrate your two moves out loud as you go.

skills.name: Identify part-to-part and part-to-whole ratio relationships

prerequisite_skill.description: Write a ratio from a described situation in the order asked (6RP3-F1)
prerequisite_skill.check_question: There are 4 red and 9 blue beads. What is the ratio of red to blue?

skills.i_do_script: A bag has 3 red marbles and 5 blue marbles. Watch me sort ratios: 3 red to 5 blue compares one PART to another PART. But 3 red to 8 marbles compares a part to the WHOLE bag -- I got 8 by adding 3 + 5. My test question is always: 'Is the second quantity a piece of the group, or the entire group?'

canonical_error.pattern: Labels a ratio part-to-whole whenever the second number is larger, instead of checking whether the second quantity names the total
canonical_error.example: Calls '3 red marbles to 5 blue marbles' part-to-whole because 5 is bigger than 3
canonical_error.why: The student judges by number size, not by what each quantity NAMES. They haven't learned that the whole is the sum of all the parts, so any big second number looks like a total to them.

redirect_script.stop: Stop -- read the labels, not the numbers.
redirect_script.prompt: Circle the two labels in the ratio. Ask: is the second label the entire group, or just one kind of thing in it? Add the parts to see what the whole would actually be.
redirect_script.praise: You checked the labels and found the whole -- that's the real test.

skills.item_template: A real-world scenario with two parts making a whole (whole numbers under 100). Student identifies which given ratio is part-to-part or part-to-whole, or classifies a single ratio. MC with 4 choices.

sample_items.stem: A fruit bowl has 6 apples and 5 oranges. Which ratio represents a part-to-part relationship?
sample_items.distractor_logic: The other three all involve the whole (11 fruits); students who key on 'apples first' may pick b

sample_items.stem: A class has 12 boys and 14 girls. Which ratio represents a part-to-whole relationship?
sample_items.distractor_logic: a and b are part-to-part; d is whole-to-part -- students who ignore order pick d

sample_items.stem: A team played 15 games and won 9 of them. The ratio 9 wins to 15 games is which kind of relationship?
sample_items.distractor_logic: part-to-part if the student thinks wins and games are two separate kinds of things instead of wins being inside the 15 games

sample_items.stem: A garden has 8 tulips and 7 roses. Which ratio compares a part to the whole?
sample_items.distractor_logic: a and b are part-to-part; d uses a wrong 'whole' of 8 -- catches students who don't add the parts

practice_problems.stem: A team has 5 wins and 2 losses. Say the part-to-part ratio of wins to losses.
A box has 4 red pens and 6 blue pens. How many pens are in the WHOLE box?
A shelf has 7 fiction and 5 nonfiction books. Which ratio is part-to-whole: 7:5 or 7:12?
practice_problems.notes: The whole (12) never appears in the story -- students must build it by adding.

practice_problems.stem: A road trip is 95 miles total, and 18 miles are done. Is '18 miles driven to 95 total miles' part-to-part or part-to-whole?
practice_problems.answer: Part-to-whole

practice_problems.stem: A student sorted a ratio. Find the mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Jar: 3 red grapes and 8 green grapes
Student wrote: 3:8 is part-to-whole because 8 is the bigger number
practice_problems.answer: 3:8 is part-to-part -- both numbers name parts (red grapes and green grapes). The whole is 3 + 8 = 11, so a part-to-whole ratio would be 3:11 or 8:11.
practice_problems.notes: Bait for the bigger-number-means-whole error.

practice_problems.stem: A class has 11 boys and 13 girls. Write the part-to-whole ratio of girls to students.
For a bag of 5 apples and 7 oranges, write one part-to-part ratio AND one part-to-whole ratio. Explain how you can tell them apart.
practice_problems.answer: Part-to-part: 5:7 (apples to oranges). Part-to-whole: 5:12 or 7:12. The part-to-whole ratio's second number counts EVERYTHING in the bag (5 + 7 = 12).

practice_problems.stem: The ratio of dogs to all pets at a shelter is 9:20. How many of the pets are NOT dogs?
practice_problems.notes: Reverses direction -- the student must use the whole to recover the other part.

activities.title: Part or Whole?
materials: One set of ratio cards per pair
activities.instructions:
1. Give each pair the cards and the two category mats.
2. Pairs read each ratio card, circle the two labels, and place the card under part-to-part or part-to-whole.
3. For every part-to-whole card, they must say the addition that builds the whole (like 4 + 5 = 9).
4. Debrief: which card fooled you, and what did the labels say that the numbers didn't?

activities.title: Build the Bag
activities.instructions:
1. One student secretly builds a 'bag' with two colors of counters (say 4 red, 6 yellow).
2. They announce ONE ratio about it -- either part-to-part ('4 red to 6 yellow') or part-to-whole ('4 red to 10 counters').
3. The group must say which kind it was and state the OTHER kind of ratio for the same bag.
4. Rotate the builder. Debrief question: how do you find the whole when nobody tells you it?

strategy_links.why: Classifying a ratio as part-to-part or part-to-whole is a quick judgment with a reason -- perfect for pair-share justification before answers are revealed.
Choral 'part-to-part!' / 'part-to-whole!' responses to rapid-fire ratio cards automatize the label check.
The bigger-number-means-whole bug is concrete and common -- students can find and fix it in seeded work.

questioning_prompts: What does the second quantity in this ratio NAME -- one kind of thing, or the entire group?
If I add all the parts, what whole do I get? Does that number appear in the ratio?
Can you turn this part-to-part ratio into a part-to-whole ratio for the same situation?
Why can't we tell part-to-whole just by looking at which number is bigger?
In '9 wins to 15 games,' are the wins inside the 15 games or separate from them?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student labels a ratio part-to-whole whenever the second number is larger, without checking what it names.
misconception_redirects.say: Circle the two labels in the ratio. Ask: is the second label the entire group, or just one kind of thing in it? Add the parts to see what the whole would actually be.
misconception_redirects.praise: You checked the labels and found the whole -- that's the real test.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student writes the whole as one of the given numbers instead of adding the parts (e.g., calls 8 the whole in '3 red and 8 green').
misconception_redirects.say: The whole has to count EVERYTHING. Add every part out loud: 3 plus 8 is 11 -- that 11 is the whole, even though the problem never said it.
misconception_redirects.praise: You built the whole yourself by adding the parts -- that's the move.

quick_checks.prompt: Thumbs up or down: '6 cats to 13 animals' is part-to-part.
quick_checks.look_for: Thumbs DOWN. A thumbs up means the student isn't reading the label 'animals' as the whole group.

quick_checks.prompt: A bin has 5 basketballs and 4 soccer balls. Say the part-to-whole ratio of basketballs to all balls.
quick_checks.look_for: 5:9 -- the student must ADD to build the 9. Answering 5:4 signals they defaulted to part-to-part; 4:9 signals a label mix-up.

worked_solution.stem: A bag has 3 red marbles and 5 blue marbles. Which ratio is part-to-whole: 3:5 or 3:8?

steps.annotation: Name what each number is -- both of these are parts, kinds of marbles.
The whole counts everything in the bag. Add all the parts to build it.
3:5 compares red to blue (two parts). 3:8 compares red to ALL marbles -- that's part-to-whole.

faded_example.stem: A parking lot has 6 cars and 4 trucks. Which ratio is part-to-whole: 6:4 or 6:10?

steps.annotation: Both numbers in the story name parts.
Add the parts to find the whole.
Decide which ratio uses the whole as its second number.

sentence_starters: This ratio is part-to-___ because the second quantity names ___.
The whole is ___ because I added ___ and ___.

vocabulary.definition: A ratio comparing one part of a group to another part, like red marbles to blue marbles.
A ratio comparing one part to the entire group, like red marbles to all marbles.
The total of all the parts added together.
A comparison of two quantities, written like 3:5, 3 to 5, or 3/5.

worked_example_script.text: Write: 'A bag has 3 red marbles and 5 blue marbles.' Underneath, list three ratios: 3:5, 3:8, 5:8.
Where could the 8 have come from? It's not in the story.
The 8 is the WHOLE bag: 3 + 5. Some ratios compare part to part; some compare a part to that whole.
So which of the three ratios compares two parts? Which compare a part to the whole?
Listen for 'part-to-whole because 5 is bigger' on 3:5. If you hear it, ask: 'What does the 5 NAME -- the whole bag, or just the blue ones?'
Circle the labels: red, blue, marbles. Draw a bracket showing red + blue = all marbles.
A class has 10 boys and 12 girls. Give me one part-to-part ratio and one part-to-whole ratio.
Last one solo: '9 wins in 15 games' -- part-to-part or part-to-whole, and how do you know?

skills.name: Identify and write equivalent ratios by multiplying both parts

prerequisite_skill.description: Multiplication facts and multiplying by one-digit numbers fluently
prerequisite_skill.check_question: What is 7 x 6? What is 9 x 4?

skills.i_do_script: The ratio 2:3 describes a recipe -- 2 scoops mix to 3 cups water. If I double EVERYTHING, 4:6, the drink tastes exactly the same. That's an equivalent ratio: multiply BOTH parts by the SAME number. Watch me test 6:9 -- 2 x 3 = 6 and 3 x 3 = 9, same multiplier, so it's equivalent. Now 4:5? I'd need x 2 on the left but there's no whole number that takes 3 to 5 -- not equivalent.

canonical_error.pattern: Adds the same number to both parts instead of multiplying both parts by the same number
canonical_error.example: Claims 3:4 is equivalent to 5:6 because 3 + 2 = 5 and 4 + 2 = 6
canonical_error.why: The student carries over additive thinking from earlier grades -- 'do the same thing to both sides' feels fair, and adding IS doing the same thing. They haven't grasped that ratios describe multiplicative relationships, so only scaling preserves them.

redirect_script.stop: Wait -- did you multiply, or add?
redirect_script.prompt: Write the multiplier over each part: what times 3 gives your new first number? What times 4 gives your new second number? Equivalent ratios need the SAME multiplier on both.
redirect_script.praise: Same multiplier on both parts -- that's exactly what makes ratios equivalent.

skills.item_template: A given ratio a:b (parts up to 20, whole numbers). Student selects all equivalent ratios from 5 options, picks the one equivalent ratio, or fills a missing part. Distractors: additive shift, flipped order, multiplier applied to one part only.

sample_items.stem: Select all ratios that are equivalent to 3:4.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 4:3 flips the order; 5:6 adds 2 to both parts; 3:8 doubles only the second part

sample_items.stem: Which ratio is equivalent to 2:5?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 4:7 adds 2 to both; 5:2 flips the order; 2:10 doubles only the second part

sample_items.stem: Select all ratios that are equivalent to 5:2.
sample_items.distractor_logic: 2:5 flips; 7:4 adds 2 to both; 15:10 multiplies the parts by different numbers (x3 and x5)

sample_items.stem: Fill in the missing value: 4:9 = 12:__
sample_items.distractor_logic: 17 if the student adds 8 to both parts; 36 if they multiply by 4 instead of 3

practice_problems.stem: Multiply both parts of 2:3 by 4. What ratio do you get?
Is 5:10 equivalent to 1:2? Answer yes or no.
practice_problems.answer: Yes

practice_problems.stem: Write two different ratios equivalent to 3:7.
practice_problems.answer: Any two whole-number multiples, like 6:14 and 9:21

practice_problems.stem: Fill in the blank: 6:10 = 3:__
practice_problems.notes: Scaling DOWN -- divide both parts by 2. Watch for 7 (subtracting 3 from both).

practice_problems.stem: A student tested two ratios. Find the mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: No, they are not equivalent. Equivalent ratios come from MULTIPLYING both parts by the same number, not adding. 4:5 doubled is 8:10, tripled is 12:15 -- 6:7 never appears, because there is no one multiplier that takes 4 to 6 AND 5 to 7 (4 x 1.5 = 6 but 5 x 1.5 = 7.5).
practice_problems.notes: Directly baits the additive error with fresh numbers.

practice_problems.stem: Which is equivalent to 9:12 -- 3:4 or 6:9?
practice_problems.notes: 9:12 divided by 3 is 3:4. 6:9 simplifies to 2:3 -- close but different.

practice_problems.stem: Find the missing value: 8:3 = __:15
practice_problems.notes: The multiplier (x5) comes from the SECOND part -- reversed direction.

practice_problems.stem: Explain why 10:15 and 14:21 are equivalent even though 10 x (a whole number) never equals 14.
practice_problems.answer: Both simplify to the same ratio: 10:15 divided by 5 is 2:3, and 14:21 divided by 7 is 2:3. (The multiplier from 10:15 to 14:21 is 1.4 -- multipliers don't have to be whole numbers.)

activities.title: Equivalent Ratio Partners
materials: One set of ratio cards per pair
activities.instructions:
1. Spread all cards face up.
2. Pairs match each ratio on the left to its equivalent partner, and must say the multiplier out loud for every match ('2:5 times 4 is 8:20').
3. Three decoy cards match nothing -- pairs must explain WHY each decoy fails (added instead of multiplied, flipped, or one part scaled).
4. Debrief: what did every decoy have in common?

activities.title: Recipe Doubling Table
materials: Two colors of snap cubes or counters
activities.instructions:
1. Build the ratio 2:3 with cubes -- 2 red, 3 blue -- as one 'batch.'
2. Build two batches, then three batches. Count each color: 4:6, then 6:9.
3. Now TRY the wrong move: add one cube to each color of a single batch (3:4). Ask: is that just a bigger batch of the same recipe? Compare 3:4 batches against 2:3 batches side by side.
4. Debrief: batches multiply the whole recipe; adding sneaks in extra of one flavor.

activities.title: Impostor Ratio
materials: Prepared sets of 4 ratios (3 equivalent + 1 impostor)
activities.instructions:
1. Show a set of four ratios, like 2:3, 4:6, 6:8, 10:15.
2. Everyone writes the impostor on their whiteboard and holds it up on your signal.
3. A correct catch only scores if the student states the multiplier test that exposes it ('6:8 is 3:4, not 2:3').
4. Let students build their own impostor sets for the group -- the best impostors use the add-the-same-number trick.
5. Debrief: why does adding the same number to both parts always break a ratio (unless the ratio is 1:1)?

strategy_links.why: A number talk on 'is 6:9 the same as 2:3?' surfaces multiplicative vs additive reasoning in students' own words.
The add-the-same-number bug is the canonical error here -- students should hunt it down in seeded work.
Rapid choral rounds ('2:3 times 4 is... 8:12!') build automaticity with the multiplier move.

questioning_prompts: What number times 3 gives 12? Does that SAME number take 4 to 16?
You doubled the first part -- what has to happen to the second part?
Why does adding 2 to both parts of 3:4 change the recipe's taste?
Can a multiplier be a fraction or decimal? What multiplier takes 10:15 to 2:3?
Two ratios are equivalent -- what one thing must be true about the multipliers?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student calls two ratios equivalent because the same number was ADDED to both parts (3:4 and 5:6).
misconception_redirects.say: Write the multiplier over each part: what times 3 gives your new first number? What times 4 gives your new second number? Equivalent ratios need the SAME multiplier on both.
misconception_redirects.praise: Same multiplier on both parts -- that's exactly what makes ratios equivalent.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student multiplies only one part (writes 2:5 = 4:5, or 2:10 for double).
misconception_redirects.say: A ratio is a package deal -- both parts ride together. If the 2 doubles, the 5 must double too. Multiply both parts and rewrite it.
misconception_redirects.praise: You scaled the whole package, both parts together -- that keeps the ratio true.

quick_checks.prompt: Fingers: is 4:6 equivalent to 2:3 -- thumbs up or down?
quick_checks.look_for: Thumbs up with 'divide both by 2' or 'times 2.' Hesitation means the student can only scale up, not down.

quick_checks.prompt: Say a ratio equivalent to 5:8 in five seconds.
quick_checks.look_for: Any correct multiple (10:16, 15:24...). Answers like 6:9 or 8:5 diagnose the additive error or a flip.

steps.annotation: Find the multiplier for the FIRST parts: 2 times 3 is 6.
Test the SAME multiplier on the second parts: 3 times 3 is 9. It matches.
One multiplier works on both parts -- that is the definition of equivalent ratios.
Find the multiplier using the first parts.
Test the same multiplier on the second parts: 5 x 4 = ?
Same multiplier on both parts? Then say whether they are equivalent.

sentence_starters: The ratios are equivalent because both parts were multiplied by ___.
These are NOT equivalent because the first part was multiplied by ___ but the second by ___.

vocabulary.definition: Ratios that describe the same relationship, made by multiplying both parts by the same number.
The one number both parts get multiplied by to scale a ratio up or down.
Staying the same -- in equivalent ratios, the relationship between the parts never changes.
Divide both parts by the same number to write the ratio with the smallest whole numbers.

worked_example_script.text: Write: 'Lemonade recipe -- 2 scoops of mix for every 3 cups of water.' Below it write 2:3 and 4:6.
If I make a double batch -- 4 scoops, 6 cups -- does the lemonade taste the same? Why?
Multiplying BOTH parts by the same number keeps the recipe in balance. That's what 'equivalent ratios' means.
Write 6:9 next to 2:3. Above the 6 write 'x 3'; above the 9 write 'x 3'. Same multiplier -- equivalent.
Now test 4:5 against 2:3. What times 2 gives 4? Does that same number take 3 to 5?
Watch for 'add 2 to both, so 4:5 works.' If it appears, pour it: 2 scoops + 3 cups vs 4 scoops + 5 cups -- ask which drink is stronger.
Give me a ratio equivalent to 5:4, and tell me your multiplier.
Solo: is 10:14 equivalent to 5:7? Prove it with a multiplier.

skills.name: Find missing values in a table of equivalent ratios

prerequisite_skill.description: Generate equivalent ratios by multiplying both parts by the same number (6RP3-S2)

skills.i_do_script: A paint table shows 2 cups blue with 3 cups green, then 4 with 6, then 6 with a blank. Watch my two moves: first I find the base ratio at the top -- 2:3. Then for the blank's row I ask 'what times 2 gives 6?' The multiplier is 3, so green is 3 x 3 = 9. Every row is just the top row times something.

canonical_error.pattern: Fills the blank by keeping a constant DIFFERENCE between the columns instead of a constant ratio
canonical_error.example: In a 2-and-3 table, sees that 3 is 1 more than 2 and fills the row with 6 as '6 and 7'
canonical_error.why: The student reads the table row-by-row looking for an adding pattern -- the habit from earlier function tables. They haven't shifted to asking 'what is each row multiplied by?', so the gap between columns looks like the rule.

redirect_script.stop: Pause -- tables like this multiply, they don't add.
redirect_script.prompt: Point to the top row and say the base ratio out loud. Now ask: what times the top number gives this row's number? Write that multiplier beside the row and use it on the other column.
redirect_script.praise: You found the row's multiplier and used it on both columns -- that's how ratio tables work.

skills.item_template: A vertical two-column table of 4 rows of equivalent ratios (whole numbers, base ratio parts 2-8) with one value replaced by '?'. Student finds the missing value. Numeric response with a data_table figure.

sample_items.stem: The table shows equivalent ratios of blue paint to green paint. What is the missing value?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 7 if the student keeps the +1 column difference from row 1; 8 if they continue the green column by +2

sample_items.stem: The table shows equivalent ratios of hours hiked to miles covered. What is the missing number of hours?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 8 if the student copies the miles-column pattern; 11 if they subtract the constant difference of 1 from 12

sample_items.stem: The table shows equivalent ratios between x and y. What is the missing value of y?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 17 if the student adds the row-3 difference (15 - 9 = 6) badly or keeps a +2 gap; 14 if they add 2 to 12

sample_items.stem: The table shows equivalent ratios of cans bought to total cost. How many cans cost $20?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 17 if the student keeps the +3 difference from row 1 (2 and 5); 7 if they continue the cans column by +1

practice_problems.stem: The base ratio in a table is 1:4. One row has x = 3. What is y in that row?
A table shows the rows 2:5, 4:10, 6:__. What is the missing value?
A ratio table shows 3:7, 6:14, 9:21, 12:__. What is the missing value?
What is the missing number of pages?
practice_problems.notes: The blank is in the FIRST column -- students must divide 24 by the base ratio's 8, or spot row 3 as 3 batches.

practice_problems.stem: A student filled in the last row of a ratio table. Find the mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Table of equivalent ratios: 2 and 3, 4 and 6, 6 and ?
Student wrote 7, because 3 is 1 more than 2, so the second column is always 1 more
practice_problems.answer: The missing value is 9. Ratio tables keep a constant MULTIPLIER, not a constant difference: the base ratio is 2:3, and 6 is 2 x 3, so the partner is 3 x 3 = 9. (Check the second row: 6 is 2 more than 4, not 1 more -- the difference was never constant.)
practice_problems.notes: Directly baits the constant-difference error with fresh numbers.

practice_problems.stem: A ratio table shows tickets and cost: 3 tickets $12, 6 tickets $24, 9 tickets $36. What is the cost of 12 tickets?
A table of equivalent ratios contains the rows 5:2 and __:6. What is the missing x-value?
practice_problems.notes: The multiplier (x3) must be found from the SECOND column and carried back to the first.

practice_problems.stem: Build your own ratio table for 4:9 with three rows, using only whole numbers under 50.
practice_problems.answer: Example: 4:9, 8:18, 12:27 (any three whole-number multiples of 4:9 with every value under 50)
practice_problems.notes: Construct-your-own reverses the direction -- the spec's At-Proficiency demand.

activities.title: The Adding Trap
activities.instructions:
1. Show the student work below. Pairs decide what rule the student THOUGHT the table followed.
2. Pairs test that rule against every row -- where does it break?
3. Pairs write the multiplier beside each row (x1, x2, x3...) and fix the blank.
4. Debrief question: what should you say to yourself every time you open a ratio table?

content.worked_problem: Ratio table: 3 and 5 / 6 and 10 / 9 and ?. A student wrote 11.
content.error_step: The student saw 5 is 2 more than 3 and decided the second column is 'always 2 more,' so 9 + 2 = 11.
content.why: Ratio tables scale by a multiplier. The base ratio is 3:5, and 9 = 3 x 3, so the partner is 5 x 3 = 15. Even the table itself disproves 'always 2 more': in row two the gap is 4, not 2.

activities.title: Batch Builder
activities.instructions:
1. Announce a recipe: 2 red cubes to 5 blue cubes is one batch.
2. Students build 1, 2, and 3 batches, counting each color into the table rows as they go: 2:5, 4:10, 6:15.
3. Cover one number with a sticky note. Partner must find it by asking 'how many batches is this row?'
4. Debrief: the multiplier IS the number of batches -- say it that way all week.

activities.title: Table Detective
activities.instructions:
1. Project a ratio table with one missing value.
2. Everyone writes BOTH the row's multiplier and the missing value on their whiteboard ('x4, so 28').
3. Show boards on the count of three. A right answer without a multiplier written scores half.
4. Every third table, seed the trap: make row 1 have a small difference (like 2 and 3) so adders produce a visibly wrong answer to discuss.

strategy_links.why: Building batches with cubes makes the multiplier concrete before students meet it as a naked number in a table.
The constant-difference bug is this skill's signature error -- students should find and fix it in seeded tables.
Pairing a correct worked table with an adder's wrong table sharpens the multiply-not-add contrast.

questioning_prompts: What is the base ratio in the top row? Say it before you touch the blank.
How many batches is this row -- what times the top number lands here?
Does your multiplier work on BOTH columns of this row?
The blank is in the first column -- which direction does your multiplier move now?
Check yourself: does the difference between the columns stay the same down the table, or grow?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student fills a blank by keeping a constant difference between the columns (writes 7 next to 6 in a 2:3 table).
misconception_redirects.say: Point to the top row and say the base ratio out loud. Now ask: what times the top number gives this row's number? Write that multiplier beside the row and use it on the other column.
misconception_redirects.praise: You found the row's multiplier and used it on both columns -- that's how ratio tables work.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student continues one column's skip-count pattern but ignores which row the blank is in (writes the next multiple regardless of the partner value).
misconception_redirects.say: The two columns are partners row by row. Cover the rest of the table: this row says 12 in the x column -- what times 3 makes 12? Use that exact multiplier on the y side.
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched the multiplier to the row instead of the column pattern -- exactly right.

quick_checks.prompt: Table rows: 2:9, 4:18, 8:__. Whisper the answer to your neighbor.
quick_checks.look_for: 36 (multiplier x4 from the base row, or doubling row 2). An answer of 22 or 27 signals difference-thinking or column skip-counting.

quick_checks.prompt: In a 3:5 table, one row starts with 15. Tell me the multiplier BEFORE the missing value.
quick_checks.look_for: 'Times 5, so 25.' Students who blurt 25 without the multiplier may be pattern-matching -- ask how they got it.

worked_solution.stem: The table of equivalent ratios shows 2:5, 4:10, 6:15, 8:__. What is the missing value?

steps.annotation: Every other row is the top row times something.

steps.math: 2 x 4 = 8, so the multiplier for this row is 4
steps.annotation: Ask: what times 2 lands on this row's 8? That's the row's batch count.
Use the SAME multiplier on the other column. The missing value is 20 -- not 17, which is what 'keep the +3 gap from row 1' would give.

faded_example.stem: The table of equivalent ratios shows 3:4, 6:8, 9:12, 15:__. What is the missing value?

steps.annotation: Name the top row first.
Find what times 3 gives this row's 15.
Multiply the other part of the base ratio by the same multiplier.

sentence_starters: The base ratio is ___, and this row is the base ratio times ___.
I knew the missing value was ___ because ___ times ___ is ___.

vocabulary.definition: A table whose rows are all equivalent ratios of the same relationship.
The simplest row of the table -- the one every other row is a multiple of.
The number of batches for a row: what the base ratio is multiplied by to make that row.
Staying the same -- in a ratio table the multiplication rule stays constant, not the gap between columns.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a two-column table labeled 'Blue (cups)' and 'Green (cups)' with rows 2-3, 4-6, 6-?, 8-12.
Before we touch the blank -- what's the ratio in the top row?
That top row is the recipe: 2 blue to 3 green. Every other row is that recipe times some number of batches.
Row two says 4 and 6. How many batches is that -- what times 2 gives 4? And does that same number take 3 to 6?
Now the blank row: it starts with 6. How many batches?
Watch for '7, because green is one more than blue.' If it appears, point at row two: is 6 one more than 4? The gap grows -- differences don't survive in ratio tables.
Write 'x 3' beside the blank row, then 3 x 3 = 9 in the blank. Write the multiplier beside every row: x1, x2, x3, x4.
Solo: a table shows 4:5, 8:10, 12:15, 20:__. Find the multiplier for the last row, then the missing value.

skills.name: Determine whether tables show the same ratio relationship

prerequisite_skill.description: Find missing values in a single ratio table using the row multiplier (6RP3-S3)
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A ratio table shows 2:7 and 6:__. What is the missing value?

skills.i_do_script: Two tables can look totally different and still describe the same relationship. Watch me test a table against 2:6, 3:9, 4:12 -- I simplify EVERY row: 2:6 is 1:3, 3:9 is 1:3, 4:12 is 1:3. One constant ratio, so any table whose rows also simplify to 1:3 -- like 5:15, 6:18 -- is the same relationship. If even one row simplifies differently, the match fails.

canonical_error.pattern: Judges that two tables match because both columns increase steadily, without checking that every row simplifies to the same ratio
canonical_error.example: Says the table 2:6, 3:9, 4:12 matches 3:7, 4:8, 5:9 because 'both tables go up by the same amount each row'
canonical_error.why: The student compares the tables' surface behavior -- growth -- instead of the invariant, the constant ratio. Any increasing table looks proportional to them because they have no row-level test to apply.

redirect_script.stop: Hold on -- growing isn't the same as matching.
redirect_script.prompt: Simplify every row of each table and write the simplified ratio beside it. The tables match only if every single row shows the same simplified ratio.
redirect_script.praise: You tested every row against one constant ratio -- that's the whole game.

skills.item_template: A reference ratio table (or a stated ratio x:y) plus four candidate tables written as row lists. Student picks the candidate with the same relationship, or constructs a table from a given ratio. MC with a data_table figure for the reference.

sample_items.stem: The table shows a ratio relationship between x and y. Which set of values has the same ratio relationship?
sample_items.distractor_logic: b is a 1:2 table (wrong constant); c keeps a +4 difference, not a ratio; d flips the relationship to 3:1

sample_items.stem: The table shows the sand-to-cement mix a mason uses. Which set of values shows the same sand-to-cement relationship?
sample_items.distractor_logic: b flips every row to 2:3; c keeps a +1 difference; d is a 3:1 table from doubling only one part

sample_items.stem: The ratio of x to y is 4:5. Which table shows ratios equivalent to 4:5?
sample_items.distractor_logic: b flips to 5:4; c adds 4 and 4 then keeps a +1 difference; d doubles only the y part, making 2:5

sample_items.stem: The table shows cups of bananas (x) and cups of berries (y) in a fruit salad. Which set of values has the same relationship between x and y?
sample_items.distractor_logic: b flips the relationship; c and d keep constant differences (+3 in c, +3 in d) instead of the constant ratio 2:5

practice_problems.stem: Do 2:3 and 8:12 show the same relationship? Answer yes or no and give the multiplier.
practice_problems.answer: Yes -- multiply both parts by 4

practice_problems.stem: Simplify every row: 5:10, 10:20, 15:30. What one ratio do all the rows equal?
Table A has rows 3:4, 6:8, 9:12. Table B has rows 4:5, 8:10, 12:15. Do they show the same relationship?
practice_problems.answer: No -- every row of A simplifies to 3:4, but every row of B simplifies to 4:5

practice_problems.stem: The ratio of x to y is 2:7. Which table matches: rows 4:14, 6:21 or rows 4:9, 6:11?
practice_problems.notes: The wrong table adds 2 to both parts of 2:7 -- the S2 bug at table scale.

practice_problems.stem: A student compared a candidate table to a given table. Find the mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Student picked 3:7, 4:8, 5:9 because both tables go up by the same amount each row
practice_problems.answer: Wrong pick. 'Both go up' is not the test -- the test is that every row simplifies to the SAME ratio. The given table's rows all simplify to 1:3. In 3:7, 4:8, 5:9 the rows simplify to 3:7, 1:2, and 5:9 -- three different ratios, so it is not even a ratio table. A correct pick would be 5:15, 6:18, 7:21.
practice_problems.notes: Baits the growth-equals-match error with fresh numbers.

practice_problems.stem: The ratio of x to y is 5:3. Write three rows of a table of ratios equivalent to 5:3.
practice_problems.answer: Example: 10:6, 15:9, 20:12 (any three whole-number multiples of 5:3)

practice_problems.stem: Two tables both contain the row 6:9. Table A also has the row 2:3; Table B also has the row 3:6. Which table shows equivalent ratios?
practice_problems.answer: Table A -- 2:3 and 6:9 both simplify to 2:3, but 3:6 simplifies to 1:2, which does not match 6:9
practice_problems.notes: Sharing one row is not enough -- every row must agree.

practice_problems.stem: Make a table that LOOKS like it grows steadily but is NOT a table of equivalent ratios, and explain what gives it away.
practice_problems.answer: Example: 2:5, 4:7, 6:9 -- each column adds 2, but the rows simplify to 2:5, 4:7, 2:3 -- different ratios, so the relationship is additive, not a constant ratio.

activities.title: Same Relationship or Not?
activities.instructions:
1. Post the anchor ratio 2:3 where everyone can see it.
2. Pairs sort each table card: same relationship as 2:3, or different.
3. Rule: before placing a card, a pair must simplify every row out loud.
4. Debrief: which card was the sneakiest, and which single row exposed it?

activities.title: Ratio Family Reunion
activities.instructions:
1. Left column lists base ratios; right column lists three-row tables.
2. Students match each base ratio to the table built from it, writing the multipliers used (x2, x3, x4) beside the match.
3. Two decoy tables match no base ratio -- students must state why.
4. Debrief: what did the decoys do instead of multiplying?

decoys: 2:8, 4:10, 6:12 (adds 2 to y after the first row)

activities.title: Whiteboard Table Court
activities.instructions:
1. Project a reference table and one candidate table.
2. Students write a verdict -- MATCH or NO MATCH -- plus the one row that proves it.
3. Boards up together; pick one MATCH and one NO MATCH student to defend their proof row.
4. Seed at least one candidate that shares its first row with the reference but drifts additively after -- the debate it starts is the lesson.

strategy_links.why: MATCH/NO MATCH verdicts with a required proof row give pairs something crisp to argue before the reveal.
Whiteboard verdicts let you scan instantly for students matching tables by growth instead of by constant ratio.
Seeded wrong verdicts (the 'both go up' bug) are the fastest way to teach the every-row test.

questioning_prompts: What does every row of the reference table simplify to?
Which single row of this candidate would you check first, and why?
Both tables grow -- why isn't that enough to call them the same relationship?
These two tables share the row 6:9. Does that guarantee they match? What else must be true?
If a table's rows simplify to three different ratios, what does that tell you about the table itself?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student declares two tables the same because both columns increase steadily, without simplifying any rows.
misconception_redirects.say: Simplify every row of each table and write the simplified ratio beside it. The tables match only if every single row shows the same simplified ratio.
misconception_redirects.praise: You tested every row against one constant ratio -- that's the whole game.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student checks only the first row of the candidate table and stops.
misconception_redirects.say: One row can be a coincidence. A ratio table has to hold its ratio in EVERY row -- check the last row too before you commit.
misconception_redirects.praise: You verified the whole table, not just the easy row -- that's real proof.

quick_checks.prompt: Does the table 4:10, 6:15, 8:20 show the same relationship as 2:5? Thumbs up or down.
quick_checks.look_for: Thumbs up with 'every row simplifies to 2:5.' A down vote usually means the student wanted to see 2:5 literally in the table.

quick_checks.prompt: Give me a three-row table equivalent to 3:8 in fifteen seconds.
quick_checks.look_for: Multiples like 6:16, 9:24, 12:32. Rows like 4:9, 5:10 diagnose the additive bug moving up from S2.

worked_solution.stem: The table shows three ratio pairs. Does the set 5:15, 6:18, 7:21 show the same ratio relationship?

steps.annotation: Simplify every row of the given table. One constant ratio: 1:3.
Simplify every row of the candidate. Same constant ratio in every row.

steps.math: All rows = 1:3, so the tables match
steps.annotation: Same relationship means every row of both tables simplifies to the same ratio -- growth alone proves nothing.

faded_example.stem: The ratio of x to y is 3:4. Does the table 6:8, 9:12, 12:15 show ratios equivalent to 3:4?
faded_example.answer: No -- the last row breaks the pattern

steps.annotation: Simplify row 1 and compare to the given ratio.
Row 2 also matches -- but keep going.
Simplify 12:15. Does it equal 3:4? Then give the verdict.

sentence_starters: Every row of the table simplifies to ___, so the constant ratio is ___.
The tables do NOT match because row ___ simplifies to ___ instead of ___.

vocabulary.definition: Staying the same -- in a true ratio table, every row simplifies to the same constant ratio.
Ratios that describe the same relationship, made by multiplying both parts by the same number.
Divide both parts of a ratio by the same number to write it with the smallest whole numbers.
The rule connecting the two quantities -- what the table is really about, underneath its numbers.

worked_example_script.text: Draw the reference table x: 2, 3, 4 / y: 6, 9, 12. Beside it write candidate A (5:15, 6:18, 7:21) and candidate B (3:7, 4:8, 5:9).
Both candidates grow -- every number gets bigger. Can we already tell which one matches the table? Why not?
Growth is cheap -- almost everything grows. The real fingerprint of the table is its constant ratio. Let's find it.
Simplify each reference row out loud and write '1:3' beside each: 2:6, 3:9, 4:12 all become 1:3.
Now simplify candidate A's rows. What do you get, row by row?
Candidate B: simplify 3:7, then 4:8. Do you even need the third row? When can you stop checking?
Watch for students matching B because 'each column goes up by 1.' Ask them to simplify 4:8 -- the 1:2 that pops out ends the debate.
Solo: the ratio of x to y is 4:5. Build me a three-row table that matches, and one row that would sneak in and ruin it.

skills.name: Plot pairs from a ratio table on the coordinate plane

prerequisite_skill.description: Plot and name points in the first quadrant (6RP3-F2 / 5.CA.11)
prerequisite_skill.check_question: To plot (3, 7), which way do you move first, and how far?

skills.i_do_script: A ratio table for 1:2 has rows 1-2, 2-4, 3-6. Watch me turn each row into an ordered pair: the first column is x, the second is y, so I get (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6). I plot each one -- right, then up -- and look at what appears: the dots line up perfectly, marching along a straight line that would pass through (0, 0). Equivalent ratios ALWAYS do that.

canonical_error.pattern: Reverses the coordinates when turning a table row into a point -- moves up by the x-value and right by the y-value
canonical_error.example: For the table row x = 2, y = 7, plots the point by going right 7 and up 2, landing on (7, 2)
canonical_error.why: The student loses the column-to-axis mapping between the table and the graph. Both numbers came from the same row, so which one is 'first' feels arbitrary -- the convention that column x is horizontal hasn't been welded to the plotting motion.

redirect_script.stop: Freeze -- which column is your sideways move?
redirect_script.prompt: Write the row as an ordered pair (x, y) BEFORE you touch the grid. Then say 'run, then jump': right the first number, up the second. Trace it with your finger first.
redirect_script.praise: Row to pair to point, right then up -- perfect translation.

skills.item_template: A ratio table (x and y columns, whole numbers fitting a 0-12 grid) and/or a first-quadrant coordinate grid. Student converts rows to ordered pairs, plots them, identifies the ratio from plotted points, or extends/spots-the-outlier on the line. MC or short response with data_table / coordinate_grid figures.

sample_items.stem: The table shows equivalent ratios between x and y. Which ordered pair is one of the points you would plot?
sample_items.distractor_logic: (2, 1) flips the first row's coordinates; (1, 4) and (4, 2) mix values from different rows

sample_items.stem: The table shows equivalent ratios. When you plot the pairs (2, 3), (4, 6), and (6, 9), what pattern do the points make?
sample_items.answer: They lie on a straight line that points through the origin
choices: They lie on a straight line that points through the origin
They form a curve that bends upward
They are scattered with no pattern
sample_items.distractor_logic: Students who plot even one pair flipped will see a false scatter; 'horizontal' comes from reading only the x-values

sample_items.stem: The plotted points show pairs from a table of equivalent ratios of x to y. What is the ratio of x to y?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 3:1 reads the coordinates in reverse; 1:2 and 2:3 misread the grid spacing

sample_items.stem: The points on the grid come from a ratio table. Which ordered pair would be the NEXT point on this line?
sample_items.distractor_logic: (7, 4) and (8, 5) continue by adding 1 to one coordinate; (4, 8) flips the correct pair

sample_items.stem: The table shows equivalent ratios. Which point does NOT belong with the plotted pairs from this table?
sample_items.distractor_logic: The first three all keep the 1:5 ratio; (6, 11) roughly doubles-plus-a-bit -- students using additive jumps may accept it

sample_items.stem: A student plotted four pairs from a 1:2 ratio table. One point was plotted incorrectly. Which one?
sample_items.distractor_logic: The other three keep y = 2x; (3, 5) is the outlier -- students who eyeball the picture without checking the ratio may pick a correct point

sample_items.stem: In the table, the first column is x and the second column is y. Which ordered pair comes from row 3?
sample_items.distractor_logic: (6, 9) flips the coordinates; (9, 4) and (6, 4) pull values from the wrong rows

sample_items.stem: Plot the pairs from the ratio table (1, 4) and (2, 8) on the grid. Describe where each point lands.
sample_items.answer: (1, 4): right 1, up 4. (2, 8): right 2, up 8. Both sit on one straight line from the origin.
sample_items.distractor_logic: Flipped plotting lands on (4, 1) and (8, 2), which makes a much flatter line

sample_items.stem: The plotted points come from a ratio table. What is the ratio of x to y shown by these points?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 1:2 and 2:1 come from counting grid squares carelessly; 1:4 misreads the axis labels

sample_items.stem: A recipe table gives the pairs (2, 6) and (4, 12). If x is on the horizontal axis, how far UP do you go for the point (4, 12)?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 4 if the student reverses the roles of the coordinates

practice_problems.stem: In the ordered pair (3, 8), which number tells you how far to move right?
A table row shows x = 2 and y = 5. Write the ordered pair you would plot.
Plot the pairs from a 1:3 ratio table -- (1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9) -- on the grid. What pattern do the points make?
practice_problems.answer: They line up on a straight line that points through the origin

practice_problems.stem: The points (2, 4), (4, 8), and (6, 12) are plotted from a ratio table. What is the ratio of x to y?
A student plotted a table row. Find the mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Student plotted the point by moving up 2 and right 7
practice_problems.answer: The student flipped the coordinates. The row (2, 7) means run RIGHT 2 along the x-axis, then jump UP 7. Their dot landed on (7, 2), a completely different point that falls off the ratio line.
practice_problems.notes: Directly baits the coordinate-flip error with fresh numbers.

practice_problems.stem: A ratio table for 3:2 gives the pairs (3, 2), (6, 4), (9, 6). Which pair comes next on the line?
A point plotted from a ratio table is (4, 10). Without seeing the table, find y when x = 8.
practice_problems.notes: Doubling x doubles y -- the graph carries the table's multiplier.

practice_problems.stem: The points (1, 4) and (3, 12) are on a ratio line. Is (2, 9) on the same line? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: No -- the ratio is 1:4, so x = 2 pairs with y = 8. The point (2, 9) sits one unit too high, off the line.

activities.title: Human Coordinate Plane
materials: Masking-tape grid on the floor (or tiles), axes labeled 0-8
activities.instructions:
1. Hand each student a card with one table row, like 'x = 2, y = 6'.
2. One at a time, students say their ordered pair out loud, then WALK it: along the wall (x-axis) first, then straight out into the room.
3. After 4-5 students stand on their points for the same table, ask the class what shape the people make.
4. Sneak in one flipped walker on purpose and let the line expose them.
5. Debrief: why do equivalent ratios make a straight line aimed at the corner (0, 0)?

activities.title: Row, Pair, Point
materials: Handout with table rows and a labeled grid A-F
activities.instructions:
1. The handout shows six table rows on the left and six lettered points plotted on a grid.
2. Pairs match each row to its point, writing the ordered pair as the middle step every time: row, then pair, then letter.
3. Two decoy points are flips of real rows -- pairs must say which rows they are flips of.
4. Debrief: what saved you from the flipped points?

decoys: Point E at (5, 1) -- flip of row (1, 5)
Point F at (6, 3) -- flip of row (3, 6)

activities.title: The Point That Fell Off the Line
materials: Printed grid showing four plotted points
activities.instructions:
1. Show the grid: points (1, 3), (2, 6), (4, 12) on a line, plus (3, 5) floating off it.
2. Pairs identify the stray point and figure out what the plotter did wrong.
3. Pairs write the corrected pair and re-plot it.
4. Debrief question: how does the LINE itself proofread your plotting for you?

content.worked_problem: A student plotted the 1:3 ratio table rows (1, 3), (2, 6), (3, 9), (4, 12). Three points made a line, but one point sits off the line at (3, 5).
content.error_step: The row (3, 9) was plotted as (3, 5) -- the student miscounted the vertical jump (or mixed the 9 with a neighboring row).
content.why: Every pair from a table of equivalent ratios lands on one straight line through the origin. A point off the line is always a plotting or table error -- here the fix is to re-plot (3, 9) on the line.

strategy_links.why: Walking the grid before drawing it is the concrete step that welds 'first number means sideways' into the plotting motion.
Narrating 'row, pair, run, jump' aloud while plotting models the exact self-talk students need at the grid.
Mini-grids on whiteboards let you scan a whole group's plots at once and spot flipped points instantly.

questioning_prompts: Turn that table row into an ordered pair before you touch the grid -- what is it?
Which number is your run, and which is your jump?
You plotted all the rows -- what do you notice about how the points sit?
If we kept the table going forever, where would the points head? Would they ever hit (0, 0)?
One of these points is off the line. What does that tell you before you check any arithmetic?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student plots a table row by moving up the x-value and right the y-value -- the point lands flipped.
misconception_redirects.say: Write the row as an ordered pair (x, y) BEFORE you touch the grid. Then say 'run, then jump': right the first number, up the second. Trace it with your finger first.
misconception_redirects.praise: Row to pair to point, right then up -- perfect translation.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student plots each point correctly but doesn't notice a stray point, or connects scattered points into a zigzag without question.
misconception_redirects.say: Points from equivalent ratios always march in a straight line aimed at (0, 0). If one dot breaks the line, the line is telling you to recheck that row.
misconception_redirects.praise: You used the line to catch your own error -- graphs proofread tables.

quick_checks.prompt: Table row: x = 5, y = 2. Point to where the dot goes on the mini-grid.
quick_checks.look_for: Right 5, up 2. A dot at (2, 5) is the flip -- have them label the axes with the column names.

quick_checks.prompt: I plotted (1, 4), (2, 8), (3, 11) from a ratio table. Quick -- do you trust my plotting?
quick_checks.look_for: 'No -- (3, 11) breaks the line; it should be (3, 12).' Trusting all three signals the student isn't using the straight-line property as a check.

worked_solution.stem: The ratio table shows the rows 1 and 2, 2 and 4, 3 and 6. Plot the pairs. What pattern appears?
worked_solution.answer: The points (1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 6) form a straight line through the origin

steps.annotation: The x-column value goes first, the y-column value second -- every row becomes one ordered pair.

steps.math: Plot (1, 2): right 1, up 2. Plot (2, 4): right 2, up 4. Plot (3, 6): right 3, up 6.
steps.annotation: Run, then jump -- the first number is always the sideways move.

steps.math: The three dots line up, aimed straight at (0, 0)
steps.annotation: Equivalent ratios always plot as a straight line through the origin -- that's the picture of 'same relationship in every row.'

faded_example.stem: A ratio table shows the rows 1 and 3, 2 and 6, 4 and 12. Plot the pairs and describe the pattern.
faded_example.answer: The points (1, 3), (2, 6), (4, 12) lie on a straight line through the origin

steps.annotation: x-column first, y-column second.
Plot each pair: run right the first number, jump up the second.
Look at the dots -- describe the pattern they make and where the line aims.

sentence_starters: The row x = ___, y = ___ becomes the point (___, ___).
The points make a straight line through the origin because ___.

vocabulary.definition: The (x, y) pairs from a table's rows that get plotted as points.
The grid made by the x-axis and y-axis where ordered pairs become points.
The point (0, 0) -- the straight line through points from equivalent ratios always aims at it.
The horizontal number line; the table's first column lives along it.
The vertical number line; the table's second column lives along it.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a two-column table (x: 1, 2, 3 / y: 2, 4, 6) next to a blank first-quadrant grid labeled 0-8 on both axes.
This table and this grid are about to become the same information. What do you think one ROW of the table turns into on the grid?
Each row becomes one ordered pair: x-column first, y-column second. Row one is (1, 2).
Plot (1, 2) slowly, narrating: 'Run right 1... jump up 2... dot.' Then hand the marker over for (2, 4).
Watch the (2, 4) plot closely -- a student who runs 4 and jumps 2 has flipped it. Have them re-say the pair with 'run' and 'jump' attached to the numbers.
Plot the last row yourself. Now look at your three dots -- what do you notice about them?
If the table had a row 0 and 0, where would that point be? Does the line aim there anyway?
Solo: here's the table x: 2, 4 / y: 3, 6. Write the pairs, plot them, and tell me whether (6, 9) would join their line.

skills.name: Solve real-world problems using tables of equivalent ratios

prerequisite_skill.description: Find missing values in a ratio table using the row multiplier (6RP3-S3)
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A ratio table shows 2:5, 4:10, 6:15. What y-value pairs with x = 8?

skills.i_do_script: A snack mix uses 2 cups of nuts for every 3 cups of pretzels, and I need to know the pretzels for 12 cups of nuts. Watch my order: FIRST I find the multiplier -- 12 divided by 2 is 6 batches. THEN I multiply the other quantity: 3 x 6 = 18 cups of pretzels. The trap is grabbing two numbers and multiplying right away -- 12 x 2 = 24 answers nothing.

canonical_error.pattern: Multiplies the target quantity by a visible number from the ratio instead of finding the multiplier first
canonical_error.example: Given 2 rides cost $5, asked the cost of 20 rides, computes 20 x 2 = $40 instead of finding the multiplier (20 / 2 = 10) and answering 10 x $5 = $50
canonical_error.why: Under word-problem pressure the student grabs the two nearest numbers and multiplies -- the ratio is treated as loose numbers instead of a paired relationship. They skip the 'how many groups of the base ratio?' question that connects the given amount to the target.

redirect_script.stop: Hold it -- multiplier first, answer second.
redirect_script.prompt: Ask the bridge question out loud: 'How many batches -- what times the ratio's number gives the amount in the problem?' Write that multiplier down, THEN use it on the other quantity.
redirect_script.praise: You found the batches first and scaled the partner quantity -- textbook ratio work.

skills.item_template: A real-world context stating a base ratio (recipes, prices, speeds; whole numbers) with a partially completed ratio table. Student extends the table to a target value (multipliers 5-12). Numeric response with a data_table figure.

sample_items.stem: A smoothie shop blends 2 cups of yogurt for every 3 cups of fruit. The table shows equivalent ratios. If the shop uses 12 cups of yogurt, how many cups of fruit does it need?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 24 if the student computes 12 x 2; 13 if they add the +1 column gap from row 1

sample_items.stem: At a fair, 2 ride tickets cost $5. The table shows equivalent ratios. How much do 20 ride tickets cost, in dollars?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 40 if the student computes 20 x 2 instead of finding the multiplier 10; 23 if they keep the +3 gap

sample_items.stem: Nadia swims 3 laps every 4 minutes. The table shows equivalent ratios. How many laps does she swim in 24 minutes?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 72 if the student computes 24 x 3; 23 if they subtract the column gap of 1 from 24

sample_items.stem: A paint mix uses 5 parts white for every 2 parts red. The table shows equivalent ratios. How many parts white are needed with 8 parts red?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 40 if the student computes 8 x 5; 11 if they keep the +3 gap from row 1

practice_problems.stem: 2 pencils cost $6. Using equivalent ratios, how much do 4 pencils cost?
3 cups of rice serve 6 people. How many people do 6 cups serve?
A car travels 120 miles on 4 gallons of gas. Extend the ratio table (4:120, 8:240, ...) to find how far it travels on 10 gallons.
practice_problems.answer: 300 miles
practice_problems.notes: Multiplier from 4 to 10 is 2.5 -- or scale down to 1 gallon (30 miles) first.

practice_problems.stem: Using the pattern in the table, how much do 9 shirts cost?
A student solved a ticket problem. Find the mistake and fix it.
shown_work: 2 rides cost $7. What do 10 rides cost?
practice_problems.answer: $35. First find the multiplier: 10 rides / 2 rides = 5 batches. Then scale the partner quantity: 5 x $7 = $35. The student multiplied the target by a number FROM the ratio instead of finding how many batches of the ratio fit.
practice_problems.notes: Directly baits the grab-and-multiply error with fresh numbers.

practice_problems.stem: A recipe uses 5 cups of flour for every 3 cups of milk. How much milk goes with 25 cups of flour?
practice_problems.answer: 15 cups

practice_problems.stem: 6 tickets cost $21. What do 8 tickets cost?
practice_problems.notes: The multiplier from 6 to 8 is not whole -- scale down to 2 tickets ($7) first, then up to 8.

practice_problems.stem: The graph of a ratio table passes through (3, 18), where x is pizzas and y is dollars. Complete the point (7, y) and say what it means.
practice_problems.answer: (7, 42) -- 7 pizzas cost $42
practice_problems.notes: Solving from the GRAPH -- the spec's 'table or graph' demand.

activities.title: Scale the Recipe
materials: Recipe card: 2 cups oats, 3 tablespoons honey (makes 1 tray)
activities.instructions:
1. Read the recipe card together: 2 cups oats to 3 tablespoons honey.
2. Announce: we need 8 cups of oats for the bake sale. Groups build the ratio table on paper down to the 8-cup row.
3. Groups measure (or mime) the scaled amounts, saying 'four batches' as they go.
4. Trap step: ask what 8 x 2 = 16 would have meant here. (Nothing -- it mixes a quantity with a ratio number.)
5. Debrief: the multiplier is the number of BATCHES, and it touches every ingredient.

activities.title: The $40 Mistake
activities.instructions:
1. Show the flawed work below. Pairs name the exact step where it went wrong.
2. Pairs draw the ratio table for 2:5 down to 20 tickets and find the real answer.
3. Pairs write one sentence: what question should the student have asked before multiplying?
4. Debrief with the class's best 'bridge question' posted on the wall.

content.worked_problem: 2 tickets cost $5. How much do 20 tickets cost? A student wrote: 20 x 2 = $40.
content.error_step: The student multiplied the 20 tickets by the ratio's 2 -- two numbers that both count tickets -- and called the result dollars.
content.why: The bridge is the multiplier: 20 / 2 = 10 batches. Ten batches of $5 is $50. Multiplying tickets by tickets can never produce dollars.

activities.title: Ratio Table Race
materials: Problem cards with a base ratio and a target
activities.instructions:
1. Deal a problem card: 'Base ratio 3 granola bars : $4. Target: 21 bars.'
2. Teams race to build the table row by row until the target row, saying each multiplier as they write it.
3. A finished table only scores if the team can answer 'how many batches did you use?' without looking.
4. Twist round: give a target that skips rows (like 30 bars) so teams must jump straight to the multiplier.
5. Debrief: which was faster, building every row or jumping by the multiplier -- and when might each be safer?

strategy_links.why: Model multiplier-first thinking, build a table together, then release -- the three-step fits this skill's fixed solution routine exactly.
Thinking aloud the bridge question ('how many batches?') before any multiplication models the self-talk that prevents number-grabbing.
A number talk on '2 tickets cost $5 -- what do 20 cost?' surfaces both the multiplier strategy and the grab-and-multiply bug for open comparison.

questioning_prompts: What is the base ratio in this story, and which of its two numbers matches the amount you were given?
How many batches -- what times the ratio's number gives the problem's amount?
You wrote a multiplication -- what are its units? Can tickets times tickets make dollars?
Could you have scaled DOWN to 1 first? When is that easier?
Where would this answer sit if the table were plotted as a graph?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student multiplies the target amount by a number from the ratio (20 rides x 2 = 40) instead of finding the multiplier.
misconception_redirects.say: Ask the bridge question out loud: 'How many batches -- what times the ratio's number gives the amount in the problem?' Write that multiplier down, THEN use it on the other quantity.
misconception_redirects.praise: You found the batches first and scaled the partner quantity -- textbook ratio work.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student pairs the multiplier with the WRONG column -- scales the same quantity they were given instead of the partner.
misconception_redirects.say: Label your columns with the story's words -- tickets, dollars. The number you were given lives in one column; your answer must come from the OTHER one.
misconception_redirects.praise: You kept each number in its own labeled column -- that's what kept the answer honest.

quick_checks.prompt: 3 apples cost $2. Tell me the multiplier for 15 apples -- just the multiplier.
quick_checks.look_for: 5 (from 15 / 3). Saying 30 or $30 means the student multiplied first and skipped the bridge question.

quick_checks.prompt: 4 laps take 6 minutes. How long do 8 laps take, and how do you know?
quick_checks.look_for: 12 minutes, 'because 8 laps is 2 batches of 4.' An answer of 48 signals target-times-ratio-number.

worked_solution.stem: A bakery uses 3 eggs for every 2 cakes. How many eggs are needed for 10 cakes?

steps.annotation: Name the ratio and label both quantities -- the given amount (10) is CAKES, so it matches the 2.
The bridge question: what times 2 cakes gives 10 cakes? Five batches -- not 10 x 3, which would mix quantities.
Use the same multiplier on the partner quantity. Five batches of 3 eggs is 15 eggs.

faded_example.stem: A garden shop sells 4 plants for $10. How much do 12 plants cost?

steps.annotation: Label the quantities -- the given 12 is PLANTS, matching the 4.
Find the multiplier: what times 4 gives 12?
Multiply the dollars by that same multiplier for the answer.

sentence_starters: The amount I was given matches the ratio's ___, so the multiplier is ___ divided by ___.
___ batches of ___ gives ___, so the answer is ___.

vocabulary.definition: A table whose rows are all equivalent ratios -- a tool for scaling a relationship up or down.
The number of batches: what the base ratio is multiplied by to reach the problem's amount.
Ratios that describe the same relationship, made by multiplying both parts by the same number.
The amount of one quantity for exactly 1 of the other -- the 1-row of the ratio table.

worked_example_script.text: Write the story: 'A smoothie shop uses 2 cups of yogurt for every 3 cups of fruit. How much fruit for 12 cups of yogurt?' Start a two-column table labeled Yogurt / Fruit with the row 2, 3.
Which column does the 12 in the question belong to? How do you know?
Someone will offer 12 x 2 = 24 or 12 x 3 = 36 immediately. Don't reject it yet -- write it in the margin and ask what its UNITS would be.
Before any multiplying, I ask the bridge question: how many batches? What times 2 cups gives 12 cups?
So the multiplier is 6. What do we do with it -- and to which number?
Write 'x 6' over both columns and fill the row: 12 and 18. Cross out the margin guesses: yogurt times yogurt can't make fruit.
Fill in the middle rows of the table (4:6, 6:9...). Do they agree with our jump straight to x 6?
Solo: 3 laps every 4 minutes -- how many laps in 20 minutes? Say your multiplier before your answer.

skills.name: Compare ratio tables and analyze errors in tables and plots

prerequisite_skill.description: Solve problems with a single ratio table (6RP3-S6) and judge whether tables match (6RP3-S4)
prerequisite_skill.check_question: Every row of a table simplifies to 3:2. Is the row 9:6 in the family? What about 8:5?

skills.i_do_script: Two trail mixes: Mix A uses 3 cups of nuts for every 2 cups of raisins, Mix B uses 5 cups of nuts for every 4 cups of raisins. Which is nuttier? I can't just say 'B, because 5 is more than 3' -- B also has more raisins. Watch me level the playing field: per 1 cup of raisins, A has 3/2 = 1.5 cups of nuts and B has 5/4 = 1.25. Same denominator, fair fight -- A is nuttier.

canonical_error.pattern: Compares two ratio tables by the raw size of their numbers instead of comparing the ratios themselves
canonical_error.example: Says the table with 9 red : 6 blue is 'more red' than the table with 6 red : 4 blue because 9 is bigger than 6 -- but both simplify to 3:2
canonical_error.why: The student treats each quantity as an absolute amount instead of half of a relationship. Bigger entries just mean more batches were mixed, not a stronger mix -- comparing ratios requires leveling to a common part (same second quantity, or a unit amount) first.

redirect_script.stop: Careful -- bigger numbers aren't a bigger ratio.
redirect_script.prompt: Level the playing field first: rewrite both ratios with the SAME second number (or find how much per 1), then compare the first numbers.
redirect_script.praise: You leveled both ratios to the same base before comparing -- that's the fair test.

skills.item_template: Two ratio relationships in context -- one shown as a data_table, the other stated in words or plotted -- with quantities under 100. Student compares strength, spots the row or point that breaks a pattern, or diagnoses another student's table-building error. MC or short response.

sample_items.stem: Mia's lemonade uses 3 lemons for every 2 cups of water, shown in the table. Leo's lemonade uses 5 lemons for every 4 cups of water. Whose lemonade has more lemons per cup of water?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Leo's is picked by students comparing raw numbers (5 > 3); 'same' comes from noticing both ratios differ by 1 -- additive thinking

sample_items.stem: The table should show equivalent ratios between x and y, but one row does not fit the pattern. Which row?
sample_items.distractor_logic: All other rows keep the 2:5 ratio; 6 should pair with 15. Students who only glance at growth see nothing wrong

sample_items.stem: Table A shows flour to eggs as 7:2, 14:4, 21:6. Table B shows flour to eggs as 2:7, 4:14, 6:21. How are the two tables related?
sample_items.answer: The quantities are switched -- Table B uses the reverse ratio of Table A
choices: The quantities are switched -- Table B uses the reverse ratio of Table A
Table B uses twice as much flour as Table A
They show the same relationship written in simpler numbers
sample_items.distractor_logic: 'Equivalent' tempts students who see the same digits; the reversal changes which quantity is large -- flipping order changes the relationship

sample_items.stem: Ava's pace is shown in the table: 8 laps every 2 songs. Ben runs 9 laps every 3 songs. Who runs more laps per song?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Ben is picked from raw comparison (9 > 8); leveling to per-song gives Ava 4 and Ben 3

sample_items.stem: A student plotted pairs from a ratio table where y is always double x. Which plotted point shows a plotting error?
sample_items.distractor_logic: The first three keep y = 2x; (5, 8) should be (5, 10) or (4, 8) -- students may excuse it because 8 is 'close'

sample_items.stem: Recipe A uses 4 cups of flour for every 1 cup of sugar. Recipe B is shown in the table. Do the two recipes have the same flour-to-sugar relationship?
sample_items.answer: Yes -- every row of B simplifies to 4:1
choices: Yes -- every row of B simplifies to 4:1
No -- B uses more flour than A
sample_items.distractor_logic: 'B uses more flour' is the raw-size error; '2:8' comes from reading one row upside down

sample_items.stem: A student built a table from the ratio 3:5 and wrote the rows 3:5, 6:8, 9:11. What mistake did the student make after the first row?
