sample_items.answer: They added 3 to both columns instead of multiplying both parts of 3:5
choices: They added 3 to both columns instead of multiplying both parts of 3:5
They multiplied only the first column
They copied the ratio upside down
sample_items.distractor_logic: The rows grow steadily, so 'nothing wrong' tempts pattern-satisfied students; checking 6:8 against 6:10 exposes the additive move

sample_items.stem: Train A travels 10 miles every 2 hours, shown in the table. Train B travels 12 miles every 3 hours. After 6 hours, how many more miles has Train A traveled than Train B?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 2 if the student compares 12 - 10 without leveling the hours; 30 or 24 if they report one train's distance instead of the difference

sample_items.stem: Two tables both start with the row 2:3. Table A's next rows multiply the row by 2 and by 3. Table B's next rows add 1 to each column. Which table shows equivalent ratios?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 'Both' tempts students who see steady growth in each; B's rows 3:4 and 4:5 are different ratios

sample_items.stem: Jar A has 6 red beads for every 4 blue beads. Jar B is shown in the table. Do the two jars have the same red-to-blue ratio?
choices: No -- Jar B has more red beads
No -- Jar B's ratio is bigger because 9 is more than 6
sample_items.distractor_logic: Choice c is the raw-size error verbatim; b confuses amount with ratio

practice_problems.stem: Simplify 12:8 and 9:6. Are they the same ratio?
practice_problems.answer: Yes -- both simplify to 3:2

practice_problems.stem: Which is stronger lemonade: 2 lemons per 1 cup of water, or 2 lemons per 2 cups of water?
practice_problems.answer: 2 lemons per 1 cup of water

practice_problems.stem: Table A has rows 4:6, 8:12. Table B has rows 6:4, 12:8. How are the two tables related?
practice_problems.answer: They are reverses -- Table B switches the two quantities of Table A (2:3 vs 3:2)

practice_problems.stem: Trail mix A uses 3 cups of nuts per 2 cups of raisins. Mix B uses 5 cups of nuts per 4 cups of raisins. Which mix has more nuts per cup of raisins?
practice_problems.answer: Mix A -- A has 1.5 cups of nuts per cup of raisins; B has 1.25
practice_problems.notes: Unit-rate comparison; the spec allows non-whole numbers exactly here.

practice_problems.stem: A student compared two bead jars. Find the mistake and fix it.
shown_work: Student: Jar B has a higher red-to-blue ratio because 9 is more than 6
practice_problems.answer: The ratios are EQUAL: 6:4 and 9:6 both simplify to 3:2. Bigger numbers only mean more total beads (more batches), not a redder mix. To compare ratios, simplify them or level them to the same number of blue beads first.
practice_problems.notes: Directly baits the raw-size comparison error with fresh numbers.

practice_problems.stem: A student built a table from 2:9 and wrote the rows 2:9, 4:11, 6:13. Find and fix the error.
practice_problems.answer: They added 2 to both columns. Correct rows: 2:9, 4:18, 6:27 -- multiply both parts of 2:9 by 2 and by 3.

practice_problems.stem: Table A shows 10 miles per 4 hours. Table B shows 12 miles per 6 hours. In 12 hours, how much farther does A travel than B?
practice_problems.answer: 6 miles -- A covers 30 miles (2.5 per hour x 12) and B covers 24 (2 per hour x 12)

practice_problems.stem: Create two ratio tables that use completely different numbers but show the SAME relationship, and prove they match.
practice_problems.answer: Example: 2:3, 4:6, 6:9 and 10:15, 20:30, 40:60 -- every row of both tables simplifies to 2:3.

activities.title: Bigger Numbers, Bigger Ratio?
activities.instructions:
1. Show the flawed comparison below. Pairs vote: is the student right?
2. Pairs build both jars with counters (6 red + 4 blue; 9 red + 6 blue) and arrange each into identical 3:2 groups.
3. Pairs write the fix: what should the student compare instead of the raw 9 and 6?
4. Debrief: when CAN you compare first numbers directly? (Only when the second numbers match.)

content.worked_problem: Jar A has 6 red beads to 4 blue. Jar B has 9 red to 6 blue. A student says Jar B is 'more red' because 9 is more than 6.
content.error_step: The student compared the raw red counts (9 vs 6) without leveling the blue counts.
content.why: Both jars simplify to 3:2 -- Jar B is just more batches of the identical mix. Ratios compare relationships, so both parts matter; level the second quantities (or simplify) before comparing the first.

activities.title: Same Mix, Reverse Mix, Different Mix
activities.instructions:
1. Post the anchor mix 3:2 (nuts to raisins).
2. Groups sort each table card into: same relationship, reverse (raisins and nuts switched), or different mix.
3. Rule: a card can't be placed until someone states the simplified ratio of one of its rows.
4. Debrief: how did you catch the reverses -- what happens to a line's steepness when a ratio flips?

activities.title: Stronger Mix Showdown
activities.instructions:
1. Project two paint-mix tables (red pigment : white base), like A = 2:5 and B = 3:5.
2. Students write which mix is redder AND their leveling move ('same white, so compare red' or 'per 1 cup').
3. Boards up together. Every few rounds, project a pair that are secretly equivalent (4:10 vs 6:15) to catch raw-number reasoning.
4. Debrief the trap rounds: what made two different-looking tables the same paint?

strategy_links.why: Setting a correct leveled comparison beside the raw-size wrong answer makes the 'fair test' visible in one glance.
Which-mix-is-stronger questions are genuine arguments -- pairs commit to a verdict and defend the leveling move before the reveal.
This skill IS error analysis -- diagnosing additive tables, flipped plots, and raw-number comparisons in others' work.

questioning_prompts: Before you compare anything: do the two ratios have the same second number? How could you make them?
What does it mean about the mixes if both tables simplify to the same ratio?
This table grows steadily -- is that enough to trust it? Which row would you audit?
The two tables use the same digits in opposite orders. Same relationship or different? Prove it.
How much of the second quantity per exactly 1 of the first? Does that settle the comparison?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student declares one table's ratio bigger because its entries are bigger numbers (9:6 beats 6:4).
misconception_redirects.say: Level the playing field first: rewrite both ratios with the SAME second number (or find how much per 1), then compare the first numbers.
misconception_redirects.praise: You leveled both ratios to the same base before comparing -- that's the fair test.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student certifies a flawed table as correct because every column grows steadily (missing an additive row like 6:8 in a 3:5 table).
misconception_redirects.say: Audit one row like an inspector: multiply the base ratio by the row's multiplier and see if the row matches. Growth is not proof -- the constant ratio is.
misconception_redirects.praise: You audited the row against the base ratio -- that's exactly how errors get caught.

quick_checks.prompt: Jar A: 4 red to 2 blue. Jar B: 6 red to 3 blue. Which jar is redder? Ten seconds.
quick_checks.look_for: 'Same -- both are 2:1.' Choosing B (because 6 > 4) is the raw-size error, this skill's core bug.

quick_checks.prompt: A table from 5:2 shows the row 10:7. Correct or broken -- and how do you know?
quick_checks.look_for: 'Broken: 10 is 5 x 2, so the partner must be 4, not 7.' Accepting it means the student isn't auditing rows with the multiplier.

worked_solution.stem: Mix A uses 3 cups of nuts per 2 cups of raisins. Mix B uses 5 cups of nuts per 4 cups of raisins. Which mix has more nuts per cup of raisins?

steps.math: A: 3 nuts / 2 raisins = 1.5 nuts per cup of raisins
steps.annotation: Level Mix A to exactly 1 cup of raisins -- divide both parts by 2.

steps.math: B: 5 nuts / 4 raisins = 1.25 nuts per cup of raisins
steps.annotation: Level Mix B the same way -- divide both parts by 4. Now both ratios have the same second number: 1.
With the raisins leveled, comparing nuts is finally fair. (Comparing the raw 5 vs 3 would have picked the wrong mix.)

faded_example.stem: Punch A uses 6 cups of juice per 3 cups of soda. Punch B uses 8 cups of juice per 4 cups of soda. Which punch is juicier?
faded_example.answer: They are the same -- both are 2 cups of juice per cup of soda

steps.math: A: 6 / 3 = 2 cups of juice per cup of soda
steps.annotation: Level Punch A to 1 cup of soda.
Level Punch B to 1 cup of soda the same way.
Compare the two per-cup amounts and state the verdict.

sentence_starters: I leveled both ratios to the same ___ before comparing, and found ___.
The tables show the same relationship because every row simplifies to ___.

vocabulary.definition: How much of one quantity for exactly 1 of the other -- the fairest way to compare two ratios.
Ratios that describe the same relationship, made by multiplying both parts by the same number.
Staying the same -- a true ratio table keeps one constant ratio in every row.
Decide which relationship is stronger -- only fair after both ratios share the same second quantity.

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for 7.RP.1 -- unit rates with fractions and complex proportional comparisons.

worked_example_script.text: Point to the printed problem: Mia's lemonade is 3 lemons for every 2 cups of water (her table reads 3:2, 6:4, 9:6). Leo's lemonade is 5 lemons for every 4 cups of water. Ask the room: whose lemonade has more lemons per cup of water?
Most hands will pick Leo because 5 lemons is more than 3. That is comparing the raw numbers -- don't correct it yet; write 'Leo, because 5 > 3' on the board as the claim to test.
Leo uses more lemons -- but what ELSE does Leo have more of than Mia? Does that make 5-against-3 a fair comparison?
Comparing 5 lemons against 3 lemons is only fair when the water matches. So let's force the water to be equal -- that move is called leveling.
Level Mia up to 4 cups of water like Leo: her 3:2 doubles to 6 lemons for 4 cups. Leo stays 5 lemons for 4 cups. Same water now -- 6 lemons beats 5.
Check it another way: how many lemons per single cup of water does each lemonade have -- what is 3 divided by 2, and 5 divided by 4?
Both the leveled table and the per-cup amount point the same way -- whose lemonade wins, and why couldn't we trust the bare 5-beats-3?
Both roads agree: Mia's 1.5 lemons per cup beats Leo's 1.25, so Mia's lemonade is more lemony. Circle Mia's as the answer.

looking_back.description: Skills the student should have but may need re-teaching.

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S3 (find the missing value in a ratio table) -- it is the heart of the standard and exposes the additive misconception immediately. If they pass, move to S5 (plotting) and S6 (solving with tables). If they fail, drop back to S1 (what a ratio compares) and S2 (equivalent ratios by multiplying). S4 and S7 are branch checks for table-level reasoning and comparison.
